title: Rising early
hook: the code asks Sikhs to rise early, bathe and remember

segments.voice: Yesterday, the daily banis: Japji, Jaap and the Swayyas at morning, Rehras at evening, Sohila at night. Your line was the code's nitnem. Which door of your day did you stop at? Day one thousand two hundred fifty-four.

The house is still dark. The street outside hasn't started yet: no buses, no phones buzzing, no one needing anything. Somewhere a tap runs, then stops. A person sits down on a folded blanket with wet hair and a covered head, and begins to say the first words of the day under their breath. Yesterday's morning prayers had to start somewhere, and the code says where: before the day starts asking. It names three things to do in that early quiet. Get up. Wash. Remember.
screen: `THE HOUSE STILL DARK.` → `A TAP RUNS, THEN STOPS.` → `GET UP. WASH. REMEMBER.`

segments.voice: In paraphrase, the code asks a Sikh to wake in the amrit vela, the ambrosial hour before dawn, to bathe, and, with the mind turned toward the one Immortal Being, to repeat the name Waheguru. The phrase amrit vela isn't new with the code. It comes from Japji Sahib itself, where Guru Nanak says that in the ambrosial hour one should reflect on the true Name and on God's greatness. And Guru Ram Das, the fourth Guru, draws a picture of a whole day around it. In his verse in Gauri, paraphrased: whoever calls themselves a Sikh of the true Guru rises early and meditates on the Name; makes the effort in those early hours and bathes; repeats the Name as the Guru teaches; and then, through the day, keeps singing the Guru's word. Notice where the picture ends. Not at dawn. It runs on into the ordinary hours. The early quiet is where the day's direction gets set. Now the second verb: bathe. That could sound like a ritual of washing. And Japji has a line that some readers hear as blunt about what water can't do. In that reading, cleansing doesn't make the mind pure, even if you wash a hundred thousand times. So the bath is not the purity. It readies the body. The remembering is the point. Get up, so that you're awake for it. Wash, so that you're present in your body for it. Then remember, before anything else gets the first word. That's the order, and the order is the teaching: the first thing the day hears is the Name.
screen: `AMRIT VELA, THE HOUR BEFORE DAWN.` · `A SIKH OF THE GURU RISES EARLY.` · `WATER DOESN'T MAKE THE MIND PURE.` · `THE FIRST WORD GOES TO THE NAME.` · then, large: `RISE AND REMEMBER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: plan to wake early once. Settle, and breathe. Choose a morning this week, and set it a little earlier than usual. Then rehearse it now. Feet on the floor. Cold water on your face. Sitting down before the phone gets picked up. What will be the first word your day hears? If you pray, you can let it be Waheguru, said slowly, a few times. If not, let it be one breath of quiet you choose on purpose. Rest in that until the bell. The bell holds the time.
Rising early. The code's morning: wake in the amrit vela, bathe, and remember the Name before the day begins. Today's word.
Your line: rise and remember. Tomorrow morning, before you look at a screen, give the first word of your day to something you'd want it to belong to. Day one thousand two hundred fifty-four.

howItsDone: Sikhs who keep the code rise in the amrit vela before dawn, bathe, and remember Waheguru before reciting the morning banis; some gurdwaras hold early morning kirtan for those who come.

what it means: the code asks Sikhs to rise in the amrit vela, bathe and remember the Name before the day begins.
what a scholar hears: amrit vela comes from Japji itself, and Guru Ram Das's portrait of a Sikh's day begins at that hour.

notes: The code's line on rising is paraphrased; the code's English rendering gives a time span before dawn for the amrit vela, which the script leaves out under the claims rule.

Japji pauri 4 (Ang 2) paraphrased as reflecting on the true Name and God's greatness in the ambrosial hour; Japji pauri 1 (Ang 1) paraphrased as cleansing not purifying the mind 'even a hundred thousand times' (the text's own figure). Please confirm both.
Guru Ram Das's verse on the Gursikh (Gauri ki Var, Ang 305) is paraphrased in part; please confirm the summary.
howItsDone says some gurdwaras hold early kirtan; please confirm.
Editor pass: Japji pauri 1 ('sochai soch...') is read by some as cleansing, by others as thinking; the teach and myth item now present the cleansing sense as one reading, not the only one.
